This is an online textbook used primarily for the course [CSA-33706 Ecological Modelling and Data Analysis](https://studyhandbook.wur.nl/modules/CSA33706?type=Cursory) at Wageningen University. It is
also designed for self-study so it may also be useful for people not attending the course.

This textbook is very much inspired and based on Benjamin Bolker's book [Ecological Models and Data in R](https://math.mcmaster.ca/~bolker/emdbook/index.html). I have mostly switched to more modern R code,
drop entirely the Bayesian component and extended hiearchical/multileve models. Note that
the style and tone of this textbook (and all the language errors I have committed) are
entirely my own as well as any mistakes and factual errors. The original book has mostly
served as guidance for which topics to focus on as we have been teaching our course with
Bolker's book for 15 years. If you really like this topic please consider checking the
original book, there are many gems in there that are worth discovering. When I read it as
a student it completely changed my mind about statistics, its relationship with modeling
(which is my true passion) and has had a big influence on my career so far.

This textbook is licensed under a [Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org). Please feel free to use it in your own teaching and modify it as
needed, you do not need my permission for that.

**AI disclaimer** - Early drafts of the different chapters and supplements were generated
in collaboration with OpenAI's Codex (specifically the GPT-5.6 series) but all the text was
revised, edited and in some cases rewritten by myself. I have very liberal attitude towards
(good) use of AI but I also understand if you may not wish to continue reading after this
statement. I do want to emphasize that the use of AI was not due to lack of expertise, I do
teaching the material in class afterall, but simply due to lack of time (and inability to
prioritise this kind of projects in the modern academic professional environment).

**How to use this online textbook**

- Use the sidebar to navigate through the the different parts. These follow the different chapters in the book (but not all chapters are covered in the course).

- Exercises are included throughout the labs as subheadings denoted [Exercise]{style="color:red; font-weight:bold;"}

- A copy of each lab is provided at the end of the sidebar with possible solutions. The solutions are given after each [Exercise]{style="color:red; font-weight:bold;"} in their own headings denoted [Solution]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}.

- The output of the different code chunks are not given and this is on purpose to prevent that you just read the material. You are meant to execute the code yourself and judge the output. Please type the code yourself rather than copy-pasting. This may seem like a waste of time but somehow the learning process is more effective when you actually type the code yourself.

- If you suspect that something went wrong, please ask your colleagues and see if you can figure out the problem together. Do not immediately ask the teachers.

**Note on how the practicals have evolved over time**

The book by Benjamin Bolker is one of a kind and still very valuable to learn the foundations of likelihood functions and the role they play in model-based inference in ecology.

However, the code use in the book and R supplement are about 20 years old at the time of writing. In the labs we have made our best efforts over the year to update the material while at the same time maintaining some level of consistency.
